At the height of Trump's trade war with China, almost every week brought new tariff announcements, and companies like Logitech responded by significantly raising prices on their products in the US.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs illegal and ordered that taxes already paid must be refunded to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing those refunds on to customers, and a class-action lawsuit is now seeking to address this situation...

Trump's Tariff Saga

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China, seemingly believing that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to bring their manufacturing back to America.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The US lacks the production infrastructure, technical expertise, and affordable labour needed to manufacture consumer electronics at the scale the major brands require.

Trump has consistently claimed that China would bear the cost of the tariffs, but the reality is that it was American companies importing goods from China who paid the tax, and those additional costs were ultimately passed on to consumers through higher prices. At the most frenzied point of this debacle, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech, for example. The company raised prices on roughly half its products by up to 25%.

Consumers Deserve a Refund

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to unilaterally impose these tariffs, and stated that the amounts already paid by American companies must be returned. The refund process is now underway.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and none of the affected companies have shown any plans to refund their customers.

The law firm CPM has now filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds on behalf of consumers who paid elevated prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The principle here is beyond dispute. The companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to customers, and now the government is refunding them. Morally, they should refund the corresponding portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought their products during that period.

However, execution is likely to be extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify all the relevant transactions across a mountain of third-party retailers, track what prices consumers paid, and calculate what proportion of that was tariff cost.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could indeed set a very interesting precedent—though it's worth noting that in class-action suits, it's only the lawyers who get rich, and the average payout to consumers is usually pitifully small.
